findings.title: Blocked addresses can be bypassed by changing email capitalization
findings.body: The lookup uses exact string equality, while signup assigns the raw `params[:email]` to the user and this model does not normalize blocked-email records. On the case-sensitive database used by the application, a block for `bad@example.com` will not match a signup using `Bad@example.com` (or capitalization changes in the local part), allowing a blocked address to register. Normalize both stored and checked addresses with the application's email canonicalization, or use a case-insensitive lookup/index.

findings.title: Match counters are inflated because validation has side effects
findings.body: `should_block?` increments and saves on every validation invocation. The signup action calls `user.valid?` before the hub registration check and then calls `user.save`, which runs validations again; consequently one blocked signup request increments `match_count` twice. Other callers that validate a record repeatedly will similarly alter the metric. Record a blocked signup attempt outside validation or otherwise ensure the statistic is updated once per request.

findings.title: Concurrent blocked-email checks lose match-count updates
findings.body: The read-modify-write sequence (`record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`) is not atomic. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked address can both read the same count and save the same incremented value, dropping one or more matches (and potentially overwriting `last_match_at`). Use an atomic database update such as `update_all`/`increment_counter` with a timestamp, or locking, when recording matches.
